name: Hypergeometric distribution
seoDesc: Hypergeometric distribution: work out probability P(X = k) from the population size and number of success states in population. A free statistics…
summary: The Hypergeometric distribution calculator turns the population size, number of success states in population and more into probability P(X = k). That makes it useful for an assignment, a report or a data discussion where you need a defensible number. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Hypergeometric distribution calculator work?
sections.html:
The Hypergeometric distribution calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports probability P(X = k) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (what to compute?); then you type in the population size (N), number of success states in population (K), the sample size (n) and number of success states in sample (k).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

sections.title: The formula behind the Hypergeometric distribution calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Probability P(X = k)=(population size (N), number of success states in population (K), sample size (n), number of success states in sample (k))
Probability P(X ≥ k)=(population size (N), number of success states in population (K), sample size (n), number of success states in sample (k))
Probability P(X ≤ k)=(population size (N), number of success states in population (K), sample size (n), number of success states in sample (k))
Probability P(X > k)=(population size (N), number of success states in population (K), sample size (n), number of success states in sample (k))
Probability P(X < k)=(population size (N), number of success states in population (K), sample size (n), number of success states in sample (k))
Mean=(number of success states in population (K) × sample size (n) ÷ population size (N))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Hypergeometric distribution calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Deciding how much confidence a sample really supports
  • Turning raw numbers into something you can quote
  • Checking a result a piece of software produced
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the population size, number of success states in population and the sample size — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Hypergeometric distribution calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns probability P(X = k), derived from the population size, number of success states in population and the sample size. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Hypergeometric distribution calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the population size, number of success states in population, the sample size and number of success states in sample, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Hypergeometric distribution calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. The calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.
